answer.label: Not Charles Darwin — a modern paraphrase by Leon C. Megginson
answer.authorDates: 1921–2010 · American professor of management & marketing, Louisiana State University
answer.sourceLine: Charles Darwin never wrote or said this line, and it does not appear in On the Origin of Species. The words are a paraphrase that business professor Leon C. Megginson coined in 1963 ↗ to summarize his reading of Darwin; over later decades it was streamlined and falsely re-quoted as Darwin’s own words.

source.excerpt: According to Darwin’s Origin of Species, it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment in which it finds itself.
trail: 1963: Leon C. Megginson delivers the paraphrase at the Southwestern Social Science Association convention, later printed in the Southwestern Social Science Quarterly ↗ — his interpretation of Darwin, not a quotation.
1960s–80s: writers drop Megginson’s hedge and recast the passage as a direct Darwin quote; the Darwin Correspondence Project ↗ documents the “slightly recast” version.
Today: the polished line is widely attributed to Darwin on posters and in textbooks, yet the Darwin Project lists it among things Darwin never said ↗.
source.excerptNote: Megginson’s original 1963 paraphrase — presented as his summary of Darwin’s ideas, without quotation marks. The familiar polished wording is a later streamlining of this passage.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full origin trail

source.rightsNote: The familiar polished wording is an anonymous streamlining with no single identifiable author, so no public-domain status can be asserted. Its closest documented source — Leon C. Megginson’s 1963 paraphrase — was published after 1930 and would itself be in-copyright to Megginson’s estate and the original publisher.

author.name: Leon C. Megginson
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1921–2010 · American professor of management & marketing, LSU
author.bio: Leon C. Megginson was a professor of management and marketing at Louisiana State University (1952–1977) and later the University of South Alabama. In a 1963 address on European lessons for American business, he paraphrased Darwin’s theory to make a point about organizational adaptability — a line that, stripped of its context and hedges, was gradually re-quoted as Darwin’s own. Megginson is now best remembered outside business scholarship for a sentence he wrote about Darwin, not one Darwin wrote.

misattribution.heading: How the misquote works
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a paraphrase promoted into a quotation — person A summarizes person B, and later the summary is re-quoted as B’s own words.

items.why: Darwin never wrote this sentence; it appears nowhere in On the Origin of Species or his other works. The Darwin Correspondence Project ↗ catalogues it as a misquotation.
Megginson offered the line as his own gloss on Darwin, without quotation marks; Quote Investigator ↗ traces the whole streamlining that turned his paraphrase into a ‘Darwin quote.’
A 1987 version oddly credited the line to the lawyer Clarence Darrow — another mistaken attribution documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought loosely echoes Darwin, but the words are Leon C. Megginson’s 1963 paraphrase — not anything Darwin wrote ↗.

context.heading: Why this quote spread
lead: The line reads like a tidy moral for a change-management slide: not strength, not brains, but adaptability wins. That is exactly why it travels — and exactly why it does not sound like Darwin, who never reduced natural selection to a motivational maxim. Darwin wrote of “natural selection” and adopted Herbert Spencer’s phrase “survival of the fittest”; “fittest” meant best-fitted to a particular environment, not strongest or smartest.

The real author was Leon C. Megginson, a Louisiana State University business professor, who in a 1963 address offered the sentence as his own interpretation of On the Origin of Species — no quotation marks. Over the following decades other writers dropped the hedge, tightened the wording, and pinned it directly on Darwin. It is now carved on the floor of a California academy of sciences and printed in countless textbooks, none of it in Darwin’s hand.
context.pull: A professor’s paraphrase of Darwin, slowly promoted into a Darwin quotation.
